title: Infectious Diseases of the Blood and Lymphatics
subject: Hematopoietic System (HEME)

overview.intro: This chapter covers infections whose main damage is done in the blood, the vessels, and the lymphatic system: the red cell parasites Babesia and Plasmodium, the blood fluke Schistosoma, the Aedes-borne arboviruses, the filoviruses, plague, cat scratch disease, and streptococcal lymphangitis. Board questions usually give an exposure, a smear or biopsy finding, and a laboratory pattern, then ask for the organism or the next complication. Each disease becomes predictable once you know where the organism lives, which host cell or vessel it injures, and whether the damage comes from the organism itself or from the host response to it.
prerequisites: Red cell structure, splenic filtration, and laboratory markers of hemolysis (HE-1 to HE-3)
Th1, Th2, and antibody effector responses, including Fc receptors and granuloma formation (IM units)
Portal venous anatomy and the causes of portal hypertension (GI units)
Coagulation cascade and disseminated intravascular coagulation (HE-6)
Lymph node architecture: follicles, paracortex, medulla, and sinuses

connections.how: Babesia and Plasmodium produce the same intravascular and extravascular hemolysis pattern taught for intrinsic and extrinsic red cell disorders.
S. mansoni is the classic cause of presinusoidal portal hypertension with preserved liver synthetic function.
S. haematobium explains why squamous cell carcinoma, rather than urothelial carcinoma, arises in the bladder in endemic regions.
Severe dengue, filovirus disease, and septicemic plague all end in vascular leak, DIC, and shock driven by cytokines.
Reading a reactive lymph node pattern correctly is the first step in separating benign enlargement from follicular and other lymphomas.

sections.title: Babesiosis: an intraerythrocytic parasite controlled by the spleen

blocks.text: Babesiosis is caused by Babesia, an apicomplexan protozoan that lives only inside red cells. In the United States the usual species is Babesia microti, carried by the black-legged (deer) tick Ixodes scapularis, the same tick that transmits Lyme disease and anaplasmosis, so coinfection is possible. Cases cluster in the Northeast and upper Midwest in late spring and summer, when nymphal ticks feed. Because the parasite lives in red cells, it also spreads by transfusion, in any season or region.

Unlike Plasmodium, Babesia has no liver stage. It enters red cells directly, divides by budding, and leaves by rupturing the cell. Multiplication is not synchronized, so fever is continuous or irregular rather than periodic, and there is no relapse from a dormant liver form. Rupture of parasitized cells causes intravascular hemolysis, and the spleen removes infected and damaged cells, adding extravascular hemolysis. The laboratory picture follows: low hemoglobin, raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, reticulocytosis, and often hemoglobinuria and mildly raised transaminases. Thrombocytopenia is common and probably reflects splenic sequestration and immune platelet destruction.
Why the spleen decides severity

Splenic macrophages remove infected red cells, and the spleen also hosts the antibody and T cell responses that control the parasite. After splenectomy, parasitemia can rise from the usual 1% to 10% to very high levels, with massive hemolysis. Older age (over about 50 years) and immunosuppression (HIV infection, cancer, organ transplantation, B cell depleting therapy such as rituximab) weaken the same defenses. In these patients the parasite burden drives cytokine release and microvascular injury, which explains acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), DIC, acute kidney injury, and heart failure. In healthy hosts, infection is often asymptomatic or a mild flulike illness, with fever up to about 40 °C (104 °F).

sections.title: Malaria: synchronized red cell rupture and the fever cycle

blocks.text: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium species transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae are the classic human species; P. knowlesi, a monkey parasite in Southeast Asia, also infects people. The mosquito injects sporozoites, which travel quickly to the liver, multiply in hepatocytes, and release thousands of merozoites. The liver stage causes no symptoms. Disease begins only when merozoites enter red cells.

blocks.title: The Plasmodium cycle in the human host
steps: Mosquito injects sporozoites into the skin and blood
Sporozoites invade hepatocytes and form liver schizonts
Liver schizonts release merozoites into the blood
Merozoites invade red cells and form ring trophozoites
Trophozoites digest hemoglobin and mature into schizonts
Schizonts rupture, releasing merozoites, pigment, and toxins
New merozoites invade fresh red cells
blocks.caption: Some merozoites become gametocytes, which infect the next mosquito. P. vivax and P. ovale also leave dormant hypnozoites in the liver.

blocks.text: Inside the red cell, each parasite passes through ring, trophozoite, and schizont stages and then ruptures the cell. Once the infection becomes synchronized, a whole cohort of schizonts ruptures together. Parasite products released at rupture, including glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchors and hemozoin, stimulate macrophages to release TNF and IL-1. These pyrogens raise prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus and reset the temperature set point. The result is a paroxysm of shaking chills, high fever up to about 40 to 41 °C (104 to 105.8 °F), then drenching sweats as the set point falls. Fever therefore recurs at the length of the red cell cycle: about 48 hours for P. vivax and P. ovale (tertian fever) and about 72 hours for P. malariae (quartan fever). Early infections and P. falciparum infections are often unsynchronized, so fever may be daily or irregular.

blocks.title: The four classic Plasmodium species
rows: Young cells (reticulocytes); entry uses the Duffy antigen
Enlarged cells with Schuffner dots; hypnozoites cause relapse
Oval, enlarged cells with fringed edges; hypnozoites cause relapse
Band-form trophozoites; low parasitemia; can persist for years; immune complex nephrotic syndrome
blocks.caption: The age of red cell a species can invade limits its maximum parasitemia, which is why P. falciparum reaches the highest burden.

blocks.text: Anemia is worse than the parasitemia predicts. Infected cells rupture, but the spleen also removes many uninfected cells whose membranes are altered or coated with antibody and complement, and TNF suppresses erythropoiesis in the marrow. The spleen enlarges because its macrophages and lymphocytes proliferate and its red pulp fills with parasitized cells; an acutely enlarged spleen, especially in P. vivax infection, can rupture. Thrombocytopenia is very common and results from splenic sequestration, immune destruction, and consumption. Lack of the Duffy antigen blocks P. vivax entry, and sickle cell trait and G6PD deficiency reduce severe falciparum disease, which explains why these traits are common in endemic regions.

blocks.predict: A patient has fevers that peak every 72 hours and later develops proteinuria and edema. Which species, and why is the parasitemia low?
blocks.explain: P. malariae has a 72-hour cycle and invades only older red cells, which limits parasitemia; chronic antigen exposure forms immune complexes that injure glomeruli.

sections.title: Plasmodium falciparum: sequestration and severe malaria

blocks.text: P. falciparum causes most malaria deaths because it combines two properties. It invades red cells of any age, so parasitemia can exceed 10%, and it makes infected cells sticky. As the parasite matures it exports P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) to knobs on the red cell surface. PfEMP1 binds endothelial receptors such as CD36, ICAM-1, and endothelial protein C receptor, and also binds uninfected red cells (rosetting). Mature trophozoites and schizonts therefore stick in small venules and capillaries of the brain, kidney, lung, gut, and placenta. Sequestration helps the parasite escape splenic clearance, but it obstructs microvascular flow and activates endothelium.

blocks.title: From sequestration to organ failure
steps: Mature parasites express PfEMP1 on red cell knobs
Infected cells adhere to venular endothelium and form rosettes
Microvascular flow falls and endothelium is activated
Local hypoxia, cytokine release, and vascular leak follow
Brain, kidney, and lung dysfunction develop
Lactic acidosis and shock in the most severe cases
blocks.caption: Damage in severe falciparum malaria comes from blocked, inflamed small vessels in the organs where infected cells sequester.

blocks.title: Complications of falciparum malaria explained by mechanism
rows: Sequestration in cerebral microvessels, endothelial activation, brain swelling
Impaired consciousness, seizures, coma; retinal changes
Rupture of many cells, splenic removal of uninfected cells, marrow suppression
Hemoglobin below about 5 g/dL in children or 7 g/dL in adults
Parasite glucose use, raised demand in fever, impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis
Glucose below about 40 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L); worse in children and pregnancy
Hypovolemia, renal sequestration, and heme pigment causing acute tubular necrosis
Massive intravascular hemolysis exceeding haptoglobin binding
Dark (blackwater) urine, low haptoglobin, high LDH
Increased pulmonary capillary permeability; acidotic breathing
blocks.caption: Lactic acidosis, shock, jaundice, and bleeding also define severe malaria. Thresholds follow WHO severe malaria criteria and are approximate.

blocks.text: The thin smear reflects sequestration. Because mature forms are stuck in vessels, peripheral blood usually shows only young ring forms and gametocytes. The rings are small and delicate, often two or more in one red cell, sometimes with two chromatin dots or flattened against the cell edge (accole forms). Infected cells are not enlarged, unlike in P. vivax and P. ovale infection. The gametocytes are crescent or banana shaped, which is unique to P. falciparum. Seeing schizonts in the peripheral blood is unusual and suggests a very heavy burden. The thick smear is more sensitive for detecting parasites, and the thin smear identifies the species and allows parasitemia to be counted.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a falciparum smear
blocks.text: A traveler returns from West Africa with fever and confusion. The thin smear shows normal-sized red cells, 12% parasitemia, many cells with two or three small rings, and a few crescent-shaped gametocytes. Step 1: normal-sized cells exclude P. vivax and P. ovale, which enlarge cells. Step 2: very high parasitemia means the parasite invades cells of all ages, which only P. falciparum does at this level. Step 3: only rings and gametocytes are visible because trophozoites and schizonts are sequestered in vessels. Step 4: sequestration in cerebral microvessels explains the confusion. Step 5: predict hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, severe hemolysis with hemoglobinuria, and kidney injury, and recognize that the low glucose may itself worsen the mental status.

sections.title: Schistosomiasis: egg granulomas in the portal and vesical veins

blocks.text: Schistosomes are blood flukes (trematodes) that live as male and female pairs inside veins. Freshwater snails release free-swimming cercariae, which penetrate intact skin during wading or bathing; a short-lived itchy rash (cercarial dermatitis) can mark the site. The young worms travel through the lungs to the portal system, mature, and then migrate to their final venous home. Adults coat themselves with host molecules and cause little harm themselves. Disease comes from their eggs.

blocks.title: The three main human schistosomes
cols: Egg spine and where eggs are found
rows: Africa, Middle East, South America, Caribbean
Hepatosplenic disease, often severe (high egg output)
blocks.caption: The location of the adult pair decides which organ the eggs damage.

blocks.text: Many eggs pass through the gut or bladder wall and leave the body; the rest are swept back in venous blood or remain in the wall. Living eggs secrete soluble antigens through their shells. The host responds with a CD4 T helper 2 (Th2) response: IL-4 drives the Th2 pattern, IL-5 recruits eosinophils, and IL-13 activates macrophages and fibroblasts. Each trapped egg becomes the center of a granuloma of eosinophils, macrophages, and lymphocytes that later heals by fibrosis. Peripheral eosinophilia reflects the same IL-5 drive. The granuloma protects tissue from egg toxins, but the cumulative scarring causes chronic disease.

blocks.title: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (S. mansoni and S. japonicum)
steps: Eggs are carried in portal blood toward the liver
Eggs lodge in small presinusoidal portal venules
Th2 granulomas with eosinophils surround each egg
IL-13 drives periportal collagen (pipestem fibrosis)
Portal venous resistance rises before the sinusoids
Splenomegaly, varices, and variceal bleeding follow
blocks.caption: Hepatocytes and sinusoids are spared, so liver synthetic function is usually preserved.

blocks.text: In the liver, fibrosis wraps the portal tracts in thick white collars, the pipestem (Symmers) fibrosis seen on cut section and ultrasound. Because the block is presinusoidal, the hepatocytes remain perfused and the lobular architecture is intact; this is not cirrhosis. Albumin and clotting factors stay near normal, and ascites and encephalopathy are uncommon until late, yet portal hypertension produces massive splenomegaly, hypersplenism with cytopenias, and bleeding esophageal varices. Once portosystemic collaterals open, eggs can bypass the liver and lodge in pulmonary arterioles, causing pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure.

In S. haematobium infection, eggs penetrate the bladder wall to reach the urine. Granulomas in the mucosa cause painless terminal hematuria, then fibrosis, calcification of the bladder wall, ureteral obstruction, and hydronephrosis. Chronic inflammation drives squamous metaplasia of the urothelium, which can progress to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, so S. haematobium is a recognized carcinogen. Weeks after a heavy first exposure, travelers can develop acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever), a systemic hypersensitivity reaction to migrating worms and early egg antigens with fever, urticaria, cough, and marked eosinophilia.

blocks.title: Worked example: portal hypertension without liver failure
blocks.text: A 30-year-old man from rural Egypt vomits blood. He has a very large spleen, eosinophilia, platelets of 80,000/microL, and normal albumin, bilirubin, and INR. Step 1: variceal bleeding with a large spleen means portal hypertension. Step 2: normal albumin and INR mean hepatocytes still work, which argues against cirrhosis, a sinusoidal process that destroys hepatocytes. Step 3: a presinusoidal block raises portal pressure while sparing the sinusoids. Step 4: eosinophilia and the region point to S. mansoni eggs trapped in portal venules with pipestem fibrosis. Step 5: low platelets reflect splenic sequestration (hypersplenism), not marrow failure.

sections.title: Dengue, chikungunya, and Zika: three Aedes-borne viruses

blocks.text: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes bite during the day and breed in small containers of standing water near homes, so all three viruses spread in tropical and subtropical cities and can circulate together. All are enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses. Dengue and Zika are flaviviruses; chikungunya is an alphavirus in the togavirus family. Their early illnesses overlap (fever, rash, aches), so the board distinction rests on what each virus targets.

blocks.title: Aedes-borne viruses compared
rows: High fever, pain behind the eyes, severe muscle and bone pain, rash
Abrupt high fever, severe symmetric polyarthralgia of small joints
Often asymptomatic or mild: itchy rash, nonpurulent conjunctivitis, arthralgia, low fever
Leukopenia, marked thrombocytopenia, rising hematocrit in severe disease
Lymphopenia; platelets usually only mildly low
Severe dengue with plasma leakage, shock, and bleeding
Joint pain lasting months to years
blocks.caption: Severe joint pain points to chikungunya, thrombocytopenia with leak to dengue, and conjunctivitis or a pregnancy risk to Zika.

blocks.text: A first dengue infection gives lasting immunity to that serotype but only brief cross-protection against the other three. Years later, antibodies from the first infection bind a second serotype without neutralizing it. The Fc portions of these antibodies attach to Fc gamma receptors on monocytes and macrophages, carrying the virus into the cells it replicates in best. This antibody-dependent enhancement raises viral load and the release of TNF and other cytokines; the viral NS1 protein also damages the endothelial glycocalyx. Infants born to immune mothers can have severe disease in a first infection because maternal antibody plays the same role.

blocks.title: Severe dengue by antibody-dependent enhancement
steps: First infection leaves antibodies to one serotype
Non-neutralizing antibodies bind a second serotype
Antibody-coated virus enters monocytes through Fc receptors
Viral load and cytokine release increase
Endothelial permeability rises around defervescence
Plasma leaks, hematocrit rises, and shock follows
blocks.caption: The dangerous critical phase usually begins as the fever breaks, about days 3 to 7.

blocks.text: Plasma leakage explains the findings of severe dengue: a hematocrit that rises as platelets fall, pleural effusions and ascites, low albumin, and narrowing pulse pressure leading to hypovolemic shock. Thrombocytopenia comes from early marrow suppression, immune-mediated platelet destruction, and consumption, and with coagulopathy it causes petechiae, mucosal bleeding, and a positive tourniquet test. Chikungunya targets synovial fibroblasts, muscle, and macrophages in joints, and persistent viral material and inflammation explain arthralgia that can last months to years. Zika infects neural progenitor cells in the fetal brain and kills them, so infection in pregnancy (highest risk in the first trimester) causes microcephaly, subcortical calcifications, eye abnormalities, and joint contractures; in adults it can trigger Guillain-Barre syndrome.

blocks.predict: In a patient with dengue on day 5, the fever has resolved, but the hematocrit has risen from 40% to 48% and the platelet count has fallen. Is the patient improving?
blocks.explain: No. A rising hematocrit with falling platelets at defervescence signals plasma leakage, the start of the critical phase that can progress to shock.

sections.title: Ebola and Marburg: filoviral hemorrhagic fever

blocks.text: Ebola and Marburg viruses are filoviruses: long, filamentous, enveloped viruses with a nonsegmented, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA genome. Fruit bats are the likely natural reservoir; the Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) is an established reservoir of Marburg virus, while the Ebola reservoir is suspected but less certain. Outbreaks start when a person handles an infected bat or primate, or bushmeat, and then spread person to person through direct contact with blood, vomit, stool, and other body fluids. Health care workers and family caregivers are at high risk, and traditional burial practices spread infection because viral loads in a body remain high after death. People are not considered infectious before symptoms begin, and virus can persist in semen and other immune-privileged sites for months after recovery. The incubation period is about 2 to 21 days.

The virus first infects monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells. Viral proteins VP35 and VP24 block type I interferon production and signaling, so the innate response fails to contain replication, and infected dendritic cells cannot activate T cells well. Infected macrophages release large amounts of TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and other cytokines and express tissue factor on their surface. Lymphocytes, though rarely infected, die in large numbers by apoptosis, producing lymphopenia and weak adaptive immunity. The virus then spreads to hepatocytes, adrenal cortical cells, and endothelium.

blocks.title: Clinical course and its mechanisms
rows: Abrupt fever, profound weakness, headache, myalgia
Infection of gut and systemic inflammation; causes hypovolemia and hypokalemia
Petechiae, bleeding from gums, venipuncture sites, and gut
DIC from tissue factor, hepatic failure of clotting factor synthesis, thrombocytopenia
Shock, confusion, kidney and liver failure
blocks.caption: Laboratory clues: early leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, AST higher than ALT, prolonged PT and aPTT, and raised D-dimer. Visible bleeding occurs in only a minority.

blocks.text: Case fatality varies by virus species and setting, averaging about 50% for Ebola and ranging from about 25% to 90% in outbreaks. Marburg disease is clinically indistinguishable from Ebola, so the history (bat caves, mines, outbreak region, contact with a sick person) and laboratory confirmation by RT-PCR separate them. Unlike dengue, filovirus disease spreads person to person and causes heavier gastrointestinal loss and liver injury.

sections.title: Plague and cat scratch disease: bacterial lymphadenitis

blocks.text: A lymph node filters lymph from a defined drainage area, so infection entering through the skin first reaches the regional node. Yersinia pestis and Bartonella henselae both enter through a skin breach and produce lymphadenitis in that node, but plague kills quickly by spreading beyond it, while cat scratch disease usually stays local and resolves.
Yersinia pestis

Y. pestis is a gram-negative coccobacillus of the Enterobacterales. With Wright, Giemsa, or Wayson stain the ends take up more dye than the center, giving the bipolar safety pin appearance. Rodents (rats; in the United States, prairie dogs and ground squirrels, mostly in the Southwest) are the reservoir, and fleas are the vector. The bacteria block the flea's foregut, so the hungry flea regurgitates bacteria into each bite. Hunters handling infected animals and owners of infected cats are also exposed.

Y. pestis survives because its virulence factors defeat phagocytes. The F1 capsule antigen resists phagocytosis, a type III secretion system injects Yop proteins that paralyze phagocytes and suppress cytokine signaling, and the plasminogen activator Pla breaks down fibrin barriers so bacteria spread from the bite. The bacteria multiply in the draining node, usually inguinal or femoral because the legs are bitten most often. After about 2 to 8 days, fever and an exquisitely tender, swollen node appear; this bubo shows hemorrhagic necrosis, neutrophils, and sheets of bacteria, and it may suppurate. Endotoxin then drives the systemic forms.

blocks.title: Spread of plague
steps: Infected flea bite inoculates Y. pestis
Bacteria reach the regional node through lymphatics
Multiplication forms a painful, necrotic bubo
Bloodstream spread causes septicemic plague with DIC
Lung seeding causes secondary pneumonic plague
Respiratory droplets cause primary pneumonic plague in contacts
blocks.caption: Septicemic plague can occur without a bubo; pneumonic plague is the form that spreads person to person.

blocks.text: In septicemic plague, endotoxin causes shock and DIC, and thrombosis of small vessels causes acral gangrene of fingers, toes, and nose. Pneumonic plague causes a rapidly progressive hemorrhagic pneumonia with bloody sputum and is the most lethal form; for this reason Y. pestis is a category A bioterrorism agent.
Bartonella henselae

B. henselae is a small, fastidious gram-negative bacillus best seen with the Warthin-Starry silver stain. Cats, especially kittens, carry it in their blood without illness, and the cat flea spreads it among cats. About 3 to 10 days after a scratch or bite, a papule or pustule forms at the site, and 1 to 3 weeks later the regional node (axillary, epitrochlear, or cervical) becomes tender and enlarged. Early the node shows follicular hyperplasia; later it shows stellate necrotizing granulomas, star-shaped zones of necrosis containing neutrophils and surrounded by palisading epithelioid histiocytes. Fever is usually mild, and the node shrinks over weeks to months. In people with advanced HIV infection the same organism instead stimulates blood vessel proliferation, causing bacillary angiomatosis.

B. henselae; gram-negative bacillus, Warthin-Starry silver stain
Rodent flea bite; handling infected animals
Cat or kitten scratch or bite

sections.title: Acute lymphangitis and reactive lymph node patterns

blocks.text: Acute lymphangitis is bacterial infection spreading along the lymphatic vessels that drain a skin wound. The usual cause is Streptococcus pyogenes (group A streptococcus), a gram-positive coccus in chains that is beta-hemolytic on blood agar. Its spreading factors, including hyaluronidase, streptokinase, and DNases, break down connective tissue matrix, fibrin, and DNA in pus, so the organism moves quickly from the wound into lymphatics. Inflamed lymphatics show through the skin as tender red streaks running proximally from the wound toward the regional nodes, for example from a hand wound toward the axilla, with tender lymphadenitis, fever, and chills. Staphylococcus aureus is a less common cause. Without control, the infection can reach the blood. A different pattern, nodular lymphangitis, with nodules along the lymphatic path, suggests organisms such as Sporothrix schenckii after a rose thorn injury.

Most enlarged lymph nodes are reactive, not malignant. The compartment that expands shows which arm of immunity is responding: follicles for B cell and antibody responses, the paracortex for T cell responses, and the sinuses for macrophages handling material carried in lymph.

blocks.title: Reactive lymphadenitis patterns
rows: B cell follicles in the cortex
Rheumatoid arthritis, early HIV infection, toxoplasmosis, syphilis
Many large germinal centers of varied size and shape
Viral infections such as infectious mononucleosis, some drugs (phenytoin), vaccination
Expanded paracortex with immunoblasts that can mimic lymphoma
Nodes draining a cancer or chronic inflammation
Granulomas, caseating or necrotizing depending on cause
blocks.caption: Mixed patterns are common; the dominant pattern guides the differential diagnosis.

blocks.text: The hardest distinction is follicular hyperplasia versus follicular lymphoma. In a normal germinal center, B cells mutate their antibody genes and switch off BCL2, an antiapoptotic protein, so cells that fail selection die and are eaten by tingible body macrophages. Reactive follicles therefore have BCL2-negative germinal centers, tingible body macrophages, and dark and light zones (polarity), and they vary in size with intact mantle zones. In follicular lymphoma, the t(14;18) translocation places BCL2 under the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter. Neoplastic germinal center cells keep BCL2 and survive, so crowded, uniform, back-to-back follicles without tingible body macrophages efface the node, and the cells express a single light chain (kappa or lambda).

blocks.title: Reactive node or lymphoma
rows: Tender, soft, mobile, often small; follows infection
Painless, rubbery or firm, often fixed; persistent or growing
blocks.caption: Tenderness signals rapid capsular stretch from inflammation; painless growth over weeks suggests neoplasia.

blocks.predict: A node biopsy shows closely packed, uniform follicles without tingible body macrophages. What will BCL2 staining of the germinal centers show, and why?
blocks.explain: It will be positive, because t(14;18) keeps BCL2 switched on in follicular lymphoma cells, which then escape the apoptosis that clears normal germinal centers.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on follicular hyperplasia versus follicular lymphoma.

integration.text: The organisms in this chapter follow a common rule: where the organism lives determines the organ that fails, and much of the damage is done by the host. Babesia and Plasmodium live in red cells, so they cause hemolysis, and the spleen, which normally clears them, both protects the host and enlarges. Schistosome eggs are trapped by vein anatomy, and Th2 granulomas with IL-13-driven fibrosis cause the portal hypertension and bladder disease. In dengue, antibodies made for protection enhance a second infection, and in filovirus disease, macrophages that should contain the virus become sources of cytokines and tissue factor that cause leak and DIC.

The lymphatic infections connect microbiology to lymph node pathology. Drainage anatomy places the bubo, the cat scratch node, and the streaks of lymphangitis, while the pattern of node enlargement shows which immune compartment responded. Histology has limits: reactive paracortical hyperplasia can mimic lymphoma and necrotizing granulomas are shared by several organisms, so exposure history, stains, clonality studies, and molecular tests are combined before a final diagnosis.

summary: Babesia infects red cells without a liver stage; small rings, rare tetrads, and no pigment distinguish it from Plasmodium, and asplenia, older age, and immunosuppression allow high parasitemia and severe hemolysis.
Malarial paroxysms occur when synchronized schizonts rupture and release products that trigger TNF and IL-1; the cycle is about 48 hours for P. vivax and P. ovale and 72 hours for P. malariae.
Malarial anemia exceeds the parasitemia because the spleen also removes uninfected cells and inflammation suppresses the marrow; splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia are common.

P. falciparum invades red cells of all ages and sequesters through PfEMP1, causing cerebral malaria, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, kidney injury, hemoglobinuria, and respiratory distress; the smear shows multiple rings and banana-shaped gametocytes.

Schistosome eggs provoke Th2 granulomas with eosinophils; S. mansoni causes presinusoidal portal hypertension with pipestem fibrosis and preserved liver function, and S. haematobium causes hematuria, bladder fibrosis, and squamous cell carcinoma.
Severe dengue follows reinfection with a different serotype through antibody-dependent enhancement, with plasma leakage shown by rising hematocrit and falling platelets.
Chikungunya causes severe, persistent polyarthralgia; Zika destroys fetal neural progenitor cells, causing congenital microcephaly.
Ebola and Marburg are filoviruses from fruit bats spread by body fluids; interferon blockade, cytokine release, and macrophage tissue factor lead to vascular leak, DIC, and multiorgan failure.

Y. pestis is a bipolar-staining coccobacillus spread by rodent fleas that forms a painful bubo and spreads to blood and lungs; B. henselae from cats causes regional lymphadenopathy with stellate necrotizing granulomas.

Streptococcal lymphangitis produces red streaks toward regional nodes; reactive follicles are BCL2 negative with tingible body macrophages, while follicular lymphoma follicles are BCL2 positive and monoclonal.
